newsitem.title: PANAMA: Big plans, few results at Central American summit.
newsitem.headline: Big plans, few results at Central American summit.

text.p: Central American heads of state were winding up their 19th Presidential Summit on Saturday, hammering out measures to boost trade but failing to agree on reforms to trim the region's institutions.
Expected talks on forging free trade between the six countries and measures to press the United States to sign a trade accord with the region were pushed to the back of the agenda.

Instead, the one-day summit saw the revival of old tensions between the Central American countries -- still recovering from Cold-War era civil wars -- preventing the leaders from reaching a decision on slashing the size and cost of regional institutions.
"These conversations are going very slowly; this is going to take quite some time (to reach an agreement)," Nicaraguan Foreign Minister Emilio Alvarez Montalvan told Reuters.

The Central American Parliament (PARLACEN) and Central American Court of Justice (CJJ) came under the toughest scrutiny for their burden on a region of 32 million people where average per capita gross domestic product ranges from $481 in Nicaragua to $2,641 in Panama per year.

"We are confronted with a unique opportunity," said Guatemala's President Alvaro Arzu. He told the summit leaders of the Central American isthmus to act with "firmness and boldness" to keep alive the process of regional integration.
These regional institutions, developed during the transition from civil wars to democracy in the early 1990s, have been lambasted as toothless and expensive talking-shops.
While officials privately acknowledged that the summit had done little to resolve long-standing differences, their public statements were upbeat.

"In these times of opportunity and challenge, where the only constant thing is change, Central America can convert itself into a region of example," Panamanian President Ernesto Perez Balladares said in a speech to open the summit.

The presidents were expected to ratify a free-trade agreement between Central America and Panama, often considered the odd-man out in issues of regional integration. Panama is currently the only country not a member of the Central American Common Market.

In preparatory talks on Friday the region's foreign ministers agreed on a resolution to work together to combat money laundering. The region's presidents also discussed ways to convince the United States to abandon plans to deport illegal immigrants back to Central America.

Attending the summit were Costa Rican President Jose Maria Figueres, Honduran President Carlos Roberto Reina, Nicaraguan President Alvaro Arzu, El Salvador's President Armando Calderon Sol, Guatemala's Arzu and Panama's Balladares.

Also attending as a guest were Dominican Republic President Lionel Fernandez, who wanted to expand his Caribbean island's commerce with Central America. Vice Prime Minister Dean Barrow, of English-speaking Belize, attended as an observer.
